content: Discussion thread for #Project announcements > An autoformalization of the sum-product counter example

Congratulations! My first questions are usually "how long did it take and how much did it cost" but it's very nice to see this formalization.yaml file which answers all of these questions and more. Just a couple of days -- wow!

Good to see a "bridge" in DedekindZeta -- what is this obsession with bridges? The Dedekind zeta stuff should almost certainly be in mathlib -- what is the plan to get it there? Or am I old-fashioned now, thinking "this formalization is suitable for mathlib and therefore it should be in mathlib"? What is the future going to look like? Mathlib is just one of many formalization projects and they're all compatible with each other and you import what you need?

I strongly recommend that this gets added to the hopscotch database and that you are forced to keep bumping. Do you have any experience in getting AI to bump? I have been bumping FLT manually using hopscotch but my gut feeling is that AI would be good at this, although of course it costs more tokens.

Something I think is missing from that announcement (and perhaps the formalization.yaml file) is the answer to the question "what is the goal of the formalization?". If it was done by an AI-for-math startup I would guess easily, but from the final frontier team of the MI I'm not sure.

What does that project bring? Checking that the result is correct, because that result is important in itself? If it's the only goal, will the project then be forgotten and rot in its repository? Is this like the many advertisement projects of the AI companies? Or is the goal also to maintain it and make the results available for other formalizations? Or is the goal to illustrate the formalization.yaml reporting in a concrete example? Or possibly several of those and many other things?
That question is not at all autoformalization-specific, and sometimes my personnal answer for my projects is "just for fun", or "because I want to unlock the formalization of stochastic calculus in Mathlib". I think it's an important piece of context.

Kevin Buzzard said:

The Dedekind zeta stuff should almost certainly be in mathlib -- what is the plan to get it there?

Well, eventually we'll want analytic continuation and functional equation via Tate's thesis, but that's still a long way off (and I think it's a student's project), so wouldn't hurt to at least get it for Dedekind zeta earlier.

1. One binding task spec, machine-decomposed. The human authored a single task file stating the deliverables for the Dedekind-zeta support library, the no-sorry/no-weakening policy, and supporting requirements as hard acceptance constraints — plus explicitly non-binding orchestrator hints (source-reading guidance, Mathlib-coverage notes, a suggested decomposition the agents were free to discard). The engine grew a task DAG from it (221 tasks), tasks spawning subtasks as the proof was refined.

I'd be curious to see that task file, as well as to learn more about the task DAG management. I've been using beads for such task DAG management very effectively locally, and would like to compare approaches.

Specifically, I prepare an overall plan in freeform text, and proceed through 3 SKILLS calls: beads-plan which interprets the plan into a proposed DAG -- I then iterate on pruning/expanding the DAG with a session; beads-commit to serialize the proposed task tree and make sure the DAG is as planned; and task-delegate which then runs subagents through the tree.

This helps retain state, prevent drift from plan or cheat by editing outside of a task boundary, and most of all, provide a level of abstraction so that it is easier to work/re-work sections.

Rémy Degenne said:

"what is the goal of the formalization?".

This question risks completely derailing the thread (because as we know some people think that using AI to do work like this, or indeed any work, is basically inherently evil so they will have strong reactions to the question) and so perhaps should be asked elsewhere. For me the answer is "let's see what AI can do, because it's only going to get better at this sort of thing".

But I think another completely reasonable answer to this question is "this is a formalization showing that a paper which was released last Friday (and which has not been refereed yet) follows from an old result which was known in the 1960s, and hence it is strong evidence that there are no errors in the paper".

Perhaps different people will see different points in it (or no point at all).

Hmm, on re-reading your question though, I see that your question is specifically for the authors, so I think that it's a totally reasonable question :-)

Sorry I'm not trying to say that any answer is wrong and not asking in an adversarial way. The answers "see what AI can do" or "formalizing that very recent paper because it's important" are both fine. It's just that I'm thinking that the reason for the formalization informs the way we should judge the result. If you tell me you just want to check that the new paper is valid, I don't care as much about the reporting about the quality and generality of the code. As long as you run it through comparator and explain to me how the challenge corresponds to the paper I'm happy.

Rémy Degenne said:

"what is the goal of the formalization?"

I think this is an important question, so let me quickly answer this. But first let me provide a bit of context (which can be deduced if you read the formalization.yaml file sufficiently carefully). The way the project progressed is as follows:

(1) The project started by reducing the main theorem (Theorem 1.1 from the paper) to three axioms: Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.2 and Equation (3.1). This was done with some very simple prompting of an off-the-shelf coding agent (claude code in this case), completely stock.
(2) We then spent some additional time filling in two of the three axioms. Equation (3.1) was proved again with standard coding agents (but a little more orchestration, see formalization.yaml).
(3) To prove Lemma 3.1, it became clear that we would need quite a lot of content about Dedekind zeta functions which didn't exist in mathlib. Here we used the orchestrator that we are building in the Formal Frontier project (this is the multi-agent system mentioned in formalization.yaml). It is currently still at the prototype stage, and this was a good opportunity to test it at a higher level of scale. The content in the DedekindZeta directory is a minimized version of what came out of that.

With this in mind, I would say that our two main goals for this were:
(a) Promoting formalization.yaml. The first phase (item (1)) is something we think essentially anyone can do with off-the-shelf tools. We want to encourage that, but also that it happens responsibly, which is why we wanted to really push formalization.yaml here.
(b) Testing out our autoformalization orchestration at larger scales. We will release it soon, but we still have some kinks to work out, and some of those became apparent when we scaled up for this project.

One last, but quite important point is that phase 3 was an example of an autoformalization that depends on an autoformalization, and we believe that this is an interesting problem! This is still at a relatively small scale, but we had to start somewhere.
Sorry if I missed this part in the formalization.yaml file, but did you clean up any of the code along the way or is this the raw output from the setup?

This is close to the raw output in the sense that there were no dedicated "cleanup" phases. The closest thing was a simple minimization pass (see here). Besides that, we also did some minimal linting, reorganization and documentation cleanup.

Yakov Pechersky said:

I'd be curious to see that task file, as well as to learn more about the task DAG management.

The task file format is what we have in https://github.com/mathlib-initiative/sum_product/tree/main/tasks

The actual large-scale Dedekind Zeta formalization took place in a different repo, with a different set of tasks, and this is what the formalization.yaml file is referring to in the comment you point to. But the format is the same. The task DAG management is, essentially: (1) ensure that task yaml files are properly formatted and (2) check the DAG structure (e.g. complete tasks can't depend on open tasks, no cycles, etc.).

This is probably going to be a controversial topic as well, but I noticed that a significant number of the spend_usd costs are simply listed as none — subscription-based usage; however my understanding (correct me if I'm wrong) is that there are still things like token limits which vary depending on the subscription tier, not to mention the cost of the subscription itself (e.g. here), and I think all this should be discussed to some extent if the intent is to be as transparent as possible.

@Bryan Wang thanks! I don't think that's a particularly controversial take! Unfortunately it's sometimes hard to get transparency about token limits associated with monthly subscriptions, and even the subscription levels/cost can get complicated (e.g. enterprise vs personal accounts add a layer of complication and are billed differently). The formalization.yaml spec is open-source, so you could add an issue aimed at future schema versions: https://github.com/mathlib-initiative/formalization.yaml

@Adam Topaz, at least for Claude and Codex, it's pretty trivial to extract the token usage from the conversation JSONL files. I routinely do this and convert to "equivalent API costs" at current pricing.
We could add this info, but my understanding is that it’s only a rough estimate. I’m not sure it’s more meaningful than giving some indication of the subscription level.

If the Dedekind zeta project was an independent thing then why is it a subdirectory rather than a second project? Is the idea of FF to show that you can have a bunch of independent repos all of which work together?

Are you committed to keeping this work up to date with mathlib?

Adam Topaz said:

We could add this info, but my understanding is that it’s only a rough estimate. I’m not sure it’s more meaningful than giving some indication of the subscription level.

It is the exact token count, for each input/output message!
